explain.title: What a syllogism is and its parts
paragraphs: Start with the word deductive. Deductive reasoning means working out whether a conclusion logically follows from some premises, where a premise is simply a statement that your reasoning starts from. Notice how narrow that job is. You are not asking whether the conclusion is likely, or whether you happen to believe it. You are asking only whether it follows, and the answer is either yes or no, with nothing in between.

A syllogism is the basic form of this kind of reasoning, and it was introduced by Aristotle. It always has the same three-part shape: two statements called premises, and then a third statement called the conclusion, which is where the reasoning arrives. So the first thing to do with any syllogism is just to sort the statements: these two are what I am given, and this last one is what I am being asked to accept.

The kind you meet first is the categorical syllogism, which describes how two categories relate to each other using the words all, no or some. Take the premises All birds are animals, and All animals eat food. The conclusion is Therefore, all birds eat food. The way to see why this works is to picture the categories as circles. The circle of birds sits completely inside the circle of animals, and the circle of animals sits completely inside the circle of things that eat food. If the small circle is inside the middle one and the middle one is inside the big one, then the small circle has to be inside the big one too. So every bird is inside the group of food eaters, and the conclusion follows. It follows because of how the categories fit inside one another, and that fit is the whole point.

People mix this up with the conditional syllogism, which begins with If p, then q instead of all, no or some. For now, keep the habit simple. Find the two premises, find the conclusion, and ask only one question: given these two premises, does the conclusion have to follow?

explain.title: How to check validity, step by step
paragraphs: Here is the uncomfortable part: there is no easy method for deciding whether a syllogism is valid. You cannot just glance at it and know. What people do instead is picture the situation the premises describe, and that is the idea behind the mental model approach of Johnson-Laird (1999). A mental model is one specific, concrete situation held in your mind that fits the premises, one way the premises could be true.

Once you have that picture, you move through it in a particular order. You build a model of the situation. Then you write down a tentative conclusion, meaning a conclusion that might hold in that picture. Then comes the step people skip, which is to hunt for an exception, a way the premises could still be true while the conclusion is false. Finally you decide. If you can find even one model where the premises are true and the conclusion is not, the conclusion has been refuted, and the syllogism is not valid. It is valid only if no model of the premises can refute the conclusion.

Walk through the students case slowly. The premises are All of the students are tired, and Some tired people are irritable. The conclusion offered is Some of the students are irritable. Picture a room of tired people. Every student is in it, because all the students are tired. But there are also tired people who are not students, and the second premise only says that some tired people are irritable. It does not say which ones. So imagine the irritable ones are all non-students. Every student is tired, some tired people are irritable, both premises are true, and yet no student is irritable. That is an exception, and one exception is enough.

This is why everything in this syllogism can sound reasonable and the syllogism is still not valid. The word some leaves open which tired people are irritable, and being tired alone does not put any student among them. The danger is stopping at the first picture that happens to fit, where the irritable people are students. A tentative conclusion often fits the first model you build, so you have to deliberately try other ways the premises could be true before you trust it.

explain.title: Validity versus truth
paragraphs: Two words get used as if they meant the same thing, and they do not. Valid describes the reasoning: a syllogism is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its two premises. True describes a statement and the world: does it match how things actually are? Validity depends on the form of the argument, while truth depends on whether the statements are correct. Validity should not be confused with truth, and that confusion is exactly what makes it hard to judge whether reasoning is logical.

The cleanest way to see the difference is to put two syllogisms side by side. The first is All birds are animals, All animals eat food, so all birds eat food. The second is All birds are animals, All animals have four legs, so all birds have four legs. Read them out loud and compare their shapes. They are built in exactly the same way, birds inside animals and animals inside a further group. Since the first has that shape and the conclusion follows, the second does too. Both are valid.

What differs is the premises. In the first, both premises are true, so the conclusion is true as well. In the second, the claim that all animals have four legs is false, and that single false premise is the only reason its conclusion is false. So here is the rule that ties it together: if a syllogism is valid and its premises are true, the conclusion must be true. But a valid form fed a false premise can still deliver a false conclusion. Validity on its own does not guarantee a true conclusion.

Truth and validity can come apart in the other direction too. In the students example, every statement sounds reasonable, yet the syllogism is not valid because the conclusion does not follow. So when you check a syllogism, do it in two separate passes. First ignore whether anything sounds true and ask only whether the conclusion follows from the premises. Then, separately, ask whether the statements are true. Keeping those two passes apart is the skill.

explain.title: Belief bias
paragraphs: Belief bias is a very human mistake. It is the tendency to think a syllogism is valid when its conclusion is believable. You read the ending, it matches what you already think, it feels right, and so you wave the whole argument through without checking whether it actually earns that ending.

The number shows how common this is: 71% of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid. That is most people. So if you catch yourself saying that one sounds right, treat that feeling as a warning rather than as evidence. Good reasoning and truth are not the same thing, and people make many errors in evaluation because of this.

Go back to the syllogism that fools people. The premises are All of the students are tired, and Some tired people are irritable. The conclusion is Some of the students are irritable. Each sentence sounds fine, and the ending is believable, because tired people being irritable is easy to accept. But now slow down and picture it. All the students are in the group of tired people. The second premise says some tired people are irritable, and that word some does not say which tired people. The irritable ones could be entirely outside the students, in which case both premises are true and no student is irritable. The conclusion does not follow, so the syllogism is not valid, however believable it sounds.

The fix is a procedure and not a feeling. Notice what your gut says about the conclusion, then set it aside on purpose. Check whether the conclusion follows from the premises by looking for an exception. Decide validity from that check and not from belief. A believable ending is exactly what makes this error easy to miss, so it is the case where you most need to run the check.

explain.title: Conditional syllogisms: the four forms cheat sheet
paragraphs: Conditional syllogisms are a second family, and they look different from the all, no and some kind. They have two premises and a conclusion, but the first premise is always of the form if p, then q. The letter p stands for a condition, and q stands for what follows when that condition is met. In the running example the first premise is If I study, I'll get a good grade, so p is studying and q is getting a good grade. Every one of the four types starts with that same sentence.

The four types differ only in what the second premise says and what is concluded from it. In type 1 the second premise is p, I studied, and you conclude q, so I'll get a good grade. In type 2 the second premise is not q, I didn't get a good grade, and you conclude not p, so I didn't study. In type 3 the second premise is q, I got a good grade, and you conclude p, so I studied. In type 4 the second premise is not p, I didn't study, and you conclude not q, so I didn't get a good grade.

Two of these four are valid and two are not. Types 1 and 2 are valid and types 3 and 4 are not. One handy way to remember the pattern is that the valid types either confirm p or deny q, while the invalid types either confirm q or deny p. Put another way, the valid ones go forward from the condition, or backward from a missing result, while the invalid ones are the reverse of that.

What makes this interesting is how people actually did. Type 1 was judged correctly 97% of the time, type 2 only 60%, and types 3 and 4 only 40% each. So the two valid forms were both judged correctly more often than the two invalid forms, but the numbers also show that valid does not mean easy. Each pair is worth taking apart one at a time, so that you understand why each one is valid or not and not just which is which.

explain.title: Modus ponens and modus tollens (the valid ones)
paragraphs: These are the two valid conditional forms, and each has a Latin name. The first premise is the same in both: If I study, I'll get a good grade. What changes is the second premise.

Modus ponens is the simple one. The second premise is I studied, so the condition is met, and the conclusion is Therefore, I'll get a good grade. In letters that is if p then q, p, therefore q. It moves forward, in the same direction as the rule. You know the studying happened, you know studying leads to a good grade, so the good grade has to follow. Nearly everyone gets this right, and 97% judged it correctly.

Modus tollens is the same rule used the other way round. The second premise is I didn't get a good grade, and the conclusion is Therefore, I didn't study. In letters that is if p then q, not q, therefore not p. The way to see why it works is to think about what would have happened if the studying had happened. The rule says a good grade would then have had to follow. There was no good grade, so the studying cannot have happened. It is exactly as valid as modus ponens.

And yet only 60% of participants judged it correctly, against 97% for modus ponens. The reason is about direction. Modus ponens runs along the rule, while modus tollens runs against it, and reasoning backward from something that did not happen is harder. So do not let the lower success rate trick you into thinking tollens is shaky. It is valid with any content, and the difficulty is in the people, not in the logic.

explain.title: Why syllogisms 3 and 4 are not valid
paragraphs: Once you accept that modus ponens and modus tollens are valid, the natural temptation is to think the other two directions work as well. They do not, and the reason is that the first premise says less than it seems to say. If p, then q tells you what happens when p is true. It does not say q happens only then, and it says nothing about what happens when p is false. Both invalid syllogisms come from reading more into the sentence than it contains.

Syllogism 3 has the premises If I study, I'll get a good grade, and I got a good grade, and it concludes Therefore, I studied. This runs from the result back to the condition. The first premise says what happens when someone studies, but it never says that studying is the only way to get a good grade. A good grade could have come from somewhere else, so the conclusion does not follow. A trick that works nicely is to put the same form with other content. If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona. I live in Arizona. Therefore, I live in Tucson. Now the problem is obvious, because a person can live in Arizona without living in Tucson. The form was never reliable, and Tucson just makes that visible.

Syllogism 4 has the premises If I study, I'll get a good grade, and I didn't study, and it concludes Therefore, I didn't get a good grade. This runs from a missing condition to a missing result. The first premise says nothing about what happens when someone does not study, and a good grade could come about some other way. It is the same kind of error as syllogism 3, only from the other side.

Both checks come down to the same question you have used all along. Can you find a case where the premises hold but the conclusion fails? If so, it is not valid. Only 40% judged each of these correctly, which makes sense, because the conclusions feel natural while the first premise supports neither of them.

explain.title: Mental models (Johnson-Laird, 1999) and the pool table
paragraphs: Mental models are the answer to the problem that there is no easy method for judging validity. The idea is that people can imagine situations, and so they can reason by picturing what the statements describe. To see that you already do this, the pool table problem shows it, and it is worth working through it slowly in your head.

The setup is this. A black ball is directly above the cue ball, and the green ball is to the right of the cue ball. A red ball is between them, meaning between the cue ball and the green ball. Then the speaker moves so that the red ball is between the speaker and the black ball. The question is which side of the speaker's line of sight the cue ball is on. Most people do not solve this with a rule. They imagine the arrangement of the balls on the table.

Here is the picture. The black ball sits above the cue ball, and the red ball and then the green ball lie off to the cue ball's right. Now stand so the red ball blocks your view of the black ball, which means you are looking past the red ball toward the black ball. From that spot, the cue ball sits off to the left. So the answer is that the cue ball is to the left of the line of sight. You got there by holding a picture in mind, not by applying a formula.

Johnson-Laird (1999) proposed that people use the same ability to solve deductive reasoning problems. A mental model is a specific situation represented in the mind, one concrete way the premises could be true. You create a model, generate tentative conclusions about it, and then look for exceptions that would falsify it. A conclusion is valid only if no model of the premises can refute it, so a single model that fits the premises but not the conclusion is enough to reject the conclusion.

explain.title: The Wason four-card problem (abstract)
paragraphs: The Wason four-card problem is a famous puzzle about testing a rule, and the difficulty is that the natural thing to do is the wrong thing. You see four cards: E, K, 4 and 7. The rule is, if there is a vowel on one side, then there is an even number on the other side. The task is to decide the minimum number of cards you must turn over to test the rule.

The principle that rescues you is the falsification principle: to test a rule, you must look for situations that falsify it. To falsify a rule is to prove it false. So instead of asking which cards fit the rule, ask for each card whether anything on its hidden side could break the rule. Go through them one at a time. The E is a vowel, so if there is an odd number behind it, the rule is broken, which means you have to turn it. The K is not a vowel, and the rule only talks about what is behind vowels, so nothing behind K can break it. The 4 is even, and an even number fits the rule whether there is a vowel or a consonant on the back, so nothing can break it. The 7 is odd, and if there is a vowel on the other side, the rule is broken, so you have to turn the 7.

The correct answer is therefore E and 7. Now look at how people did. 46% of participants said the 4 needed to be turned over, which is an error, and only 7% said the 7 did, which is the correct choice. The 4 is tempting because an even number is what the rule seems to be about, and finding a vowel behind it would feel like a success. But a success does not test anything, since the rule could not have failed there.

The point is that most participants fail to look for falsifying cases. They look for evidence that agrees with the rule instead of the one situation that would break it. That is why so few picked the 7.

explain.title: Concrete Wason version and permission schemas
paragraphs: The same puzzle gets dramatically easier when it is stated in everyday terms. In the concrete version, the rule is if drinking beer, then 21 years old, and the four cards read beer, soda, 16 years old and 21 years old. 73% of participants answered this version correctly, compared with 7% who found the 7 in the vowel version. When the problem is stated in concrete everyday terms, correct responses greatly increase.

Apply the same falsification question you used on the letters. For each card, could its hidden side break the rule? The only case that breaks the rule is someone drinking beer who is under 21. So the beer card must be turned, because the person's age might be under 21. The 16 years old card must be turned too, because the drink might be beer. The soda card cannot break the rule, since the rule says nothing about people drinking soda. And the 21 years old card cannot break it either, because someone who is 21 is allowed to drink anything. So you turn beer and 16 years old.

Why is this easier? The explanation is the permission schema, which is the idea that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. A schema is a familiar pattern of knowledge, and a permission schema is the pattern of a rule that grants permission once a condition is met. In the beer rule, being 21 years old is the condition, and drinking beer is what can then be carried out. People are familiar with rules like this, and the rule tells them exactly what to check: if someone is drinking beer, check their age, and if someone is 16, check what they are drinking. The abstract rule about vowels and even numbers does not call up this familiar pattern, so people do not know what to look for.

The logical form is the same in both problems. Two cautions apply. Context is important, because the same problem becomes easier in a familiar setting. But familiarity is not always important, so familiarity alone does not explain the improvement. What helps is a context that brings up a permission schema.

explain.title: Framing effect: gain versus loss
paragraphs: The framing effect is the finding that decisions are influenced by how a decision is stated. The wording of a choice can highlight one aspect of the situation, such as what might be gained or what might be lost, and the facts can stay exactly the same while the wording changes what people focus on. Tversky and Kahneman (1981) studied how framing changes the amount of risk people accept. When situations are framed in terms of gains, people tend toward a risk-aversion strategy, which means they prefer the sure option. When they are framed in terms of losses, people tend toward a risk-taking strategy, which means they prefer the gamble.

The disease problem shows this. A disease is expected to kill 600 people, and two programs have been proposed. In the first version the outcomes are described in terms of people saved, which makes it the gain frame. Program A: 200 people will be saved for certain. Program B: a 1/3 probability that 600 people will be saved and a 2/3 probability that no people will be saved. 72% of people chose Program A, the sure option, and 28% chose Program B. So most people avoided the risk, even though the gamble could save everyone.

In the second version the same disease is expected to kill 600 people, but the outcomes are described in terms of people who will die, which makes it the loss frame. Program C: 400 people will die for certain. Program D: a 1/3 probability that no one will die and a 2/3 probability that 600 people will die. This time 78% of people chose Program D, the gamble, and 22% chose Program C.

Now compare the two versions carefully, because this is the heart of it. If 200 of 600 people are saved, then 400 die, so Program C has the same outcome as Program A. And Program D is the very same gamble as Program B. Nothing about the outcomes changed. Only the wording changed, yet most people switched from the sure option to the gamble. A statement about lives saved points to what can be gained, while a statement about deaths points to what can be lost, and that shift in attention is what moved people.
